newsitem.title: SPAIN: Peseta could weather possible rate cut with aplomb.
newsitem.headline: Peseta could weather possible rate cut with aplomb.

text.p: The peseta will remain sturdy even if the Bank of Spain responds to a sharp fall in the inflation rate with a cut in its key interest rate soon, analysts said on Friday.
The peseta is firmly supported by dollar strength and expected tourist receipts as the summer season approaches and by long-term interest rates.
"The rise in the dollar is going to maintain the stability of the peseta," Carlos Mazario, economist at AFI, said.
Analysts said the onset of the tourist season could put pressure on the peseta to appreciate in coming months. Tourism provided Spain with income of some 3.5 trillion pesetas last year.
The peseta is likely to remain in its current range between 84.20 and 84.7O, even after a possible rate cut at the Bank of Spain's next repo auction on April 15.
By midday on Friday, the peseta was trading at 84.25/26 against the mark, compared with 84.43/45 late on Thursday and 84.51/52 a week ago.
The dollar has soared some 12 percent against the mark this year, helping buoy European currencies against the German currency including the peseta.
"We don't think the peseta is going to make any sharp moves (including if the central bank cuts its official rate)," said Mazario.
Spain's consumer price index (CPI) rose a modest 0.1 percent in March to give a 2.2 percent rise on the year -- the lowest rate in 29 years.
Analysts said the data could prompt the Bank of Spain to sanction its third official money market rate cut of the year as soon as April 15.
But this is unlikely to concern the peseta and it should also shrug off a possible correction in the debt market, analysts said.
"The peseta is much more related to long-term interest rates than to repos," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale.
Yields on the 7.35 percent 10-year benchmark Spanish bond are trading at about 6.90 percent.
"There is some risk of profit-taking (in the bond market) because the recent rise has been very strong, but we see the peseta stable within a range of 84.30 and 84.70," said Urrutia.
The 10-year spread between Spanish bonos and German Bunds narrowed to 96 basis points after Friday's inflation data from around 130 bps at the end of March.
But traders said the strength was unlikely to be sharp enough to prompt the Bank of Spain to intervene.
The Bank of Spain intervened heavily at the beginning of the year to keep the peseta from strengthening past 84.00 per mark.
